text: This place is older than grief. Before the continent you just left was even a dream,
there was Moo. And the beings of Moo were, by every measure that matters, the opposite of
what came after. They were simple, the teachers say, a somewhat primitive people,
if you measure by tools and towers. But their inner life was advanced beyond anything their
rough hands could build. They had the one thing every later civilization would trade everything
to recover. They were at peace with being small inside of vast creation. And that peace
made them luminous. It was, by all accounts, a helpful and harmless place. No wars gouged
its history. No weapons learned to in make bodies. They lived. They loved the land and each other.
They watched the sky with wonder, rather than ambition. Picture their days as best you can.
Mornings given to the tending of gardens and children, mid days to craft and song,
evenings to the quiet councils where the elders listened more than they spoke.
They had little use for haste. What they valued, attention, kindness, the keeping of promises,
does not fossilize. So the archaeologist will never dig it up. But the teachers insist it was real
and that its reality mattered more than any monument. And then the earth itself moved.
The plates of the world shifted. The ocean rose over their home and move went down.
Through no action of their own. No one was to blame. That is the hardest kind of loss to hold.
The kind with no lessen attached. Only absence. Those who survived scattered north and south
across the great continents. And their blood runs in the indigenous peoples of the Americas
and the far north to this day. The guides say that when you feel an unexpected tenderness towards
those first peoples, towards their patience and their listening, you are remembering kin.
You are remembering move. It is worth asking why they came here at all. The records say these
souls were drawn from a world whose aging sun could barely hold life any longer. A whole people
transplanted across the gulfs between stars because their old home was dying. And they chose this
younger planet the way you might choose a garden to tend it, not to own it. There is something
unspeakably moving in that. Refugees from a spent sun given a second world who spent it in gentleness.
The teachers want you to consider that the experiment of mood did not fail. It completed. A
people lived well, loved well, and left without wreckage. The ocean took their land, but it could
not take what they were. What they were went into the bloodlines, into the dreams, into the quiet
knowing that a human life can be simple and still be whole. There is something the teachers want
you to feel here in the quiet of these drowned stones. That a civilization can be great without
being grand. Mew never reached for the infinite with machines. It bowed to the infinite with
attention. The stones here are soft with age and with the patient work of the sea. Nothing here
accuses. If Atlantis is the warning, Mew is the benediction. Proof that the experiment of being
human was at least once, gentle all the way through. Hold that proof carefully. It is
rarer than you think. Drift a while. Let the water move you the way time moves everything.
Without hurry, without malice. And when you are ready, carry one thing back to the surface.
The knowledge that simplicity is not the absence of advancement. Sometimes it is advancement finished.
The far shore that all the striving was trying to reach. Mew is gone. What it knew is not.
The next time you are tempted to measure a life by its monuments, remember the drowned
continent that built none. And was, by the only measure that survives the water, the most advanced of
the more.
